Database.//: Off by default: with more than one replica, concurrent instances would race to migrate. Enable per environment, or run migrations as a separate deploy step.

Network.//: Addresses of reverse proxies whose X-Forwarded-For may be believed. Empty means the client address comes from the connection. Anything listed here can choose the address used for rate-limiting and audit, so list only proxies you operate.

RateLimit.//: Credential attempts allowed from one client address per window — sign-in and the password-reset pair. Counts every attempt, not only failures, so everyone behind one connection shares one allowance: a crew signing in at shift change through a site router, or a mobile carrier's CGNAT. Measured with scripts/loadtest-login.sh: the CPU ceiling is roughly 80 sign-ins a second on four cores, so 120 a minute is far from a denial-of-service risk and covers a hundred-person shift change. Lower it where every client has its own address.

RefreshCookie.//: How the refresh token reaches a browser. SameSite Strict makes the cookie its own CSRF defence and works when the API and the admin panel share a registrable domain (api.example.com and admin.example.com are same-site). A genuinely cross-domain deployment needs None, which requires HTTPS and re-opens CSRF — putting the two on one domain is the better fix.
RefreshCookie.//Path: Must cover the refresh route the clients call, which is versioned: /api/v1/auth/refresh. A browser matches a cookie path as a prefix, so the earlier /api/auth was stored and never sent, and the panel signed the operator out on every reload. Widening it to /api would put a seven-day credential on every API request; a second API version changes this value instead.
RefreshCookie.Name: construction.refresh

Retention.//: How long finished-with data is kept, in days. LocationRecordDays is the one that matters: a minute-by-minute record of where an employee was is personal data, and at one ping a minute per person the table grows by roughly a million rows a month per hundred workers. Set it to 0 to keep everything, which the API warns about at startup.

Serilog.//: Console output is plain text here so a developer can read it. Set Serilog:WriteTo:0:Args:formatter to Serilog.Formatting.Compact.CompactJsonFormatter, Serilog.Formatting.Compact for a deployment, so a log collector can parse fields instead of scraping a line. The file sink is a fallback for a single-host install; in a container it is written to a layer that disappears with the container, which is why shipping to an aggregator is the real answer.
